beats.narration_text: Eleven episodes of teaching a system to read what executives say. This one asks a question the system had never asked about itself: how long is any of it good for? I'm Anjana.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself
runningText 'measuring shelf life…'
output lines resolve, already answered

props.command: ECIS produces a graded signal from every earnings call. But a signal has a shelf life, and some of them must go stale faster than others. Can it measure how long each signal type stays predictive, work out why its own confident calls were wrong, and drop the features that stopped earning their place?
output: every signal type gets a measured half-life
confident-but-wrong predictions, clustered by root cause

beats.narration_text: ECIS extracts financial guidance signals from earnings calls using four readers and a five-dimensional triangulator. The prediction layer forecasts guidance direction, and a revision predictor uses six models to flag likely changes. Episode 11 added Q&A dodge detection with cross-encoder reranking, competitive positioning with a three-classifier ensemble, a guidance revision predictor, fine-tuned Sentence-BERT embeddings, and a FinBERT ensemble. This week: not every signal ages the same way. Some decay in days. Some last for months. Phase 17 measures signal shelf life, catches false positives, reads the structure behind management language, and prunes the feature set.

props.sparkLine: Not every signal ages the same.

beats.narration_text: Different signals lose predictive power at different rates. The signal decay module measures correlation with excess returns at horizons from one day to sixty days. Each signal type gets a half-life — the point where its predictive value drops below significance. The hedging index might hold for twenty days. Dodge scores may fade in five. The system uses these half-lives to weight recent data appropriately — fast-decaying signals count for less at longer horizons.

show.event: axes draw; the 0.5 threshold line appears across them
six decay curves draw left to right, each at its own rate
markers land where each curve crosses the threshold
the legend fills with each signal's half-life
hedging index highlights — holds for twenty days
dodge score highlights — gone in five

beats.narration_text: High confidence does not guarantee accuracy. The false positive analysis module examines every prediction where confidence exceeded zero point seven but the direction was wrong. It clusters the errors by root cause — ambiguous language, sarcasm misread, section misattribution, context-dependent phrases, or unusual market conditions. Signals matching known patterns get a reduced confidence modifier. At the same time, multi-quarter signal chaining tracks trends across consecutive calls. Three quarters of rising hedging with declining confidence is no longer three independent readings. It's a sustained deterioration signal.

beats.narration_text: A fine-tuned DeBERTa classifier sorts every management statement into speech act types: promises, commitments, hedged intentions, predictions, deflections, and assertions. The distribution reveals whether management is making concrete commitments or filling time with vague intentions. Discourse structure analysis goes deeper — it maps how the narrative is organized. Deflection pivots away without addressing the negative. Each pattern is a signal about how management wants you to hear the story.

beats.narration_text: As the feature set grows, not every feature earns its place. Automated feature selection runs three methods — recursive feature elimination, permutation importance, and LASSO shrinkage — and flags features that rank in the bottom ten percent across all three for removal. Feature interaction discovery identifies synergistic combinations: high dodge score plus rising hedging plus defensive language predicts outcomes better than any feature alone. These interaction features are added to the vector. Embedding drift monitoring tracks whether the Sentence-BERT space is shifting and flags when re-fine-tuning is needed.

beats.narration_text: Phase 17 added signal decay half-lives, false positive filtering, multi-quarter signal chains, transcript quality gates, speech act classification, discourse structure analysis, metaphor tracking, sarcasm detection, automated feature selection, interaction features, and embedding drift monitoring. The system doesn't just extract signals anymore. It measures how long they last, catches when they're wrong, reads the structure behind the language, and prunes its own feature set. props.sparkLine: How long does a signal last?

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Eleven episodes built a system that extracts signals. Every signal type now has a measured shelf life, so a reading that was good yesterday isn't assumed to be good next month. Every confident prediction that turned out wrong gets clustered by why, and signals matching a known failure pattern are marked down before they're used. Management language gets read for its structure — what kind of statement was that, and where in the story was the bad news put. And the feature set is pruned by three methods that have to agree, which is the part most teams skip.

props.artifactHeading: A system that doubts its own signals.
artifactLines: Each signal type gets a half-life measured against excess returns from one day out to sixty; fast-decaying signals are weighted down at longer horizons.
Confident-but-wrong predictions are clustered by root cause, and signals matching a known failure pattern take a confidence penalty.
Multi-quarter chaining turns three consecutive readings into one sustained deterioration signal rather than three independent ones.
A fine-tuned DeBERTa classifier sorts statements into speech acts, and discourse analysis maps where in the narrative the bad news was placed.
Features must rank in the bottom tenth on recursive elimination, permutation importance AND LASSO to be dropped; embedding drift is monitored for retrain.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the uncomfortable one. Most of us build a score and then never ask how long it stays true, or go back and look at the times it was confident and wrong. Take a score you already produce and do both. Paste this into Claude and press hardest on the second part, because a list of your own confident failures, sorted by cause, is the most useful thing you can build this month — and the least pleasant.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Your turn.'; prompt types itself
runningText 'auditing your score…'

props.command: I produce a score or a prediction that people act on — a risk score, a lead score, a forecast, a health metric. Can you help me: one, work out how I'd measure how long that score stays predictive, and what it would mean if the answer were days rather than months; two, design a way to collect every case where the score was confident and wrong, and cluster those by root cause rather than by magnitude; and three, tell me honestly which of my inputs I could drop entirely without losing anything, and how I'd prove it?
